subtype: Approach: app limits and removing triggers [Action]
passage:
Sunday. Lavanya sat on her bed with her phone and deleted the short-video apps one by one. She capped messaging at a fixed time each day, turned off every notification that wasn't from family, and moved her games to the computer in the hall, where she'd need to walk over and choose them.
Wednesday. At nine in the evening her thumb reached for the phone by itself. There was nothing to open. She felt restless and a bit bored. She texted her brother Rafiq: “bored.” He replied, “Come play carrom.” She did.
Sunday again. Homework had been finished before dinner three days in a row. The weekly report showed a lot fewer hours, and she looked at the number for a while.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling on Wednesday at nine?
qa.a: Restless and a bit bored: her thumb reached for the phone and there was nothing to open.

qa.q: What else could Lavanya do if the urge stays strong, and why?
qa.a: Plan something to do at that hour every evening, since removing the apps leaves a gap that something else needs to fill.

qa.q: How does Wednesday's text look to Rafiq?
qa.a: Rafiq gets a one-word message from his sister and offers something to do together, and may feel needed and glad to help.

grounding: A student deletes short-video apps, limits messaging, mutes notifications and moves games to a computer.

passage:
Hrithik, you keep asking how I get so much done without looking at my phone. I wasn't born like this. When I was in Class Eleven, my mother used to say, “Jahnavi, that phone owns you.” She was right.
One Sunday I made a list and did everything on it in one sitting. First, I deleted the two short-video apps. Not logged out; deleted. Second, I set a one-hour daily limit on messaging, so after that the app went grey. Third, I turned off every notification except calls and my mother's messages. Fourth, the hardest: I moved my games off the phone onto the old family computer in the drawing room. If I wanted to play, I had to walk there, switch it on and wait. Usually I decided I didn't want to that much.
Did I become perfect? No. But my phone got boring, and boring was exactly what I needed. So, Hrithik, start with the notifications. That one's easiest.

qa.q: Where did young Jahnavi move the games?
qa.a: Onto the old family computer in the drawing room.

qa.q: How did young Jahnavi seem to feel once the phone got boring?
qa.a: Jahnavi seemed relieved, even pleased, because a boring phone was exactly what was needed.

qa.q: Which step in the story made games a deliberate choice, and why did it work?
qa.a: Moving them to the family computer, because walking there and waiting gave time to decide it wasn't worth it.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi's mother have seen the change back then?
qa.a: The mother, who used to say the phone owned Jahnavi, would likely have been relieved and surprised to see it set aside.

grounding: An elder recalls deleting short-video apps, limiting messaging, turning off notifications and moving games to a computer so playing became a deliberate choice.

passage:
Preeti couldn't just put the phone away. Her coaching classes ran on it, with the timetable, the recorded lectures and the test links, and the family had no laptop. So on Saturday she tried something else, with her brother Saurabh reading out the settings.
She deleted the short-video app and the one with endless reels. She put a forty-five-minute daily limit on messaging, enough for the class groups. She switched off every notification except calls, coaching and her parents. The two games she loved went onto Saurabh's old tablet, which lived in the steel cupboard; playing meant asking for the key.
On Monday she opened the phone for a lecture, and nothing else lit up. On Wednesday the messaging app went grey at 8 pm. She sighed and went back to her notes.
By Friday she had asked for the cupboard key only once.

qa.q: What daily limit did Preeti put on messaging?
What does Preeti's sigh on Wednesday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests mild frustration and disappointment when the app went grey, but she accepted the limit and went back to her notes.

qa.q: Why did removing triggers suit Preeti better than putting the phone away?
qa.a: Her classes needed the phone, so cutting apps and alerts kept the useful parts while making the rest harder to reach.

qa.q: What is the arrangement like for Saurabh?
qa.a: Saurabh becomes keeper of the cupboard key, a small role that shows he is in on the plan and quietly supporting it.

grounding: Shows a student deleting short-video apps, limiting messaging, turning off notifications and moving games off her phone so they need a deliberate choice.
